claims.text: Partial routing profiles solo traces of a lead and a worker model: an LLM annotator labels recurring subtasks, an LLM judge scores quality, and the measured cost and quality are compiled into delegation tiers that go into the lead's prompt.
On held-out ViBench at delta 0.75, partial routing beats the lead alone on score at lower cost.
On Terminal-Bench, partial routing at delta 0.75 has the highest pass rate of any method at roughly the lead's cost.
Task-level routers, including a hindsight oracle, score lower at higher cost than partial routing on ViBench.
Giving the lead only the subtask plan, with no worker, cuts cost at a similar or higher score.
Unguided delegation to a cheaper worker already produces much of the ViBench gain; the profile adds a smaller increment on held-out applications.
Judge quality scores are stable across re-runs relative to the gaps between the models.
The method needs no weight changes, so it applies to proprietary API models and can be recompiled when models update.
With a second model pair, partial routing improves on the lead alone on Terminal-Bench, but on ViBench it trades some score for a large cost reduction.

limits_authors.text: The main results use one model pair per benchmark with a small number of held-out tasks and runs.
The second-pair runs lack the other baselines and repeated runs.
Gains are untested for pairs with smaller capability or price gaps.
Sensitivity to rho, tau and the number of profiling tasks is not determined.
The LLM annotator and judge were not validated against human labels.
The authors did not check whether the lead followed its assigned tiers.

likely_overclaims: The headline delta is the best setting chosen on the held-out results, even though the authors recommend choosing delta on a validation set; lower delta settings score below the lead alone on ViBench.
The margin over unguided delegation on held-out ViBench is small and rests on few runs; the much larger margin on the profiling applications is in-sample.
The Terminal-Bench gains rest on a small number of tasks run twice, so the differences amount to only a few tasks.
The Limitations say the second-pair runs show gains carry over, but on the second ViBench pair partial routing scores below the lead alone.
The context-management explanation for the worker gains is a hypothesis that the paper does not test.

figures.caption: Figure 1: Partial routing. Offline, the lead and the worker each do the same tasks alone, and an LLM annotator then tags each step of their rollouts (gray) with a recurring subtask from a set \mathcal{S}; an LLM judge scores both models on each subtask, and \delta turns quality and cost saving into delegation tiers.
Figure 2: Cost and quality on the ten held-out ViBench applications, mean of three runs.
Figure 3: Cost and pass rate on the 23 held-out Terminal-Bench tasks, mean of two runs per task.

change_for_agents: Agent builders can profile logged solo traces of a strong and a cheap model by subtask and put the resulting delegation tiers into the lead's prompt. In this paper that made delegation cheaper and often better without any training. Even passing along just the subtask plan may cut cost.

compact.claim: Prompt-level delegation tiers built from profiled solo traces let a frontier lead model delegate subtasks to a cheaper worker, beating the lead alone and task-level routing on held-out coding benchmarks.
compact.method: An LLM annotator labels recurring subtasks in solo rollouts of both models, and an LLM judge scores each model's quality per subtask. Cost savings and quality risk are combined with a parameter delta into delegate, conditional or keep tiers, which go into the lead's prompt alongside a delegation tool.

results.finding: ViBench score rises from 70.2 to 78.5 at 19% lower cost at delta 0.75
Terminal-Bench pass rate of 60.9%, versus 54.3% for the lead alone and for unguided delegation
Plan alone cuts cost by 39% on ViBench and 16% on Terminal-Bench

compact.limits: Evidence comes from one main model pair per benchmark with few held-out tasks and runs, and the settings and LLM labels were not validated with sensitivity sweeps or human labels.
